segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not judge, so that you will not be judged.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For by the judgment you judge with, you will be judged, and by the measure you measure with, it will be measured to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ and look, the beam is in your own eye?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls in front of pigs, or they may trample them under their feet and turn and tear you apart.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or is there anyone among you who, when his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or when he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So if you, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in the heavens give good things to those who ask him!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So whatever you want people to do for you, do just that for them as well; for this is the Law and the Prophets.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and spacious the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For narrow is the gate and constricted the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inside are rapacious wolves.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: By their fruits you will recognize them. People do not gather grapes from thornbushes, or figs from thistles, do they?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way, every good tree produces fine fruit, but the rotten tree produces bad fruit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a rotten tree produce fine fruit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Every tree that does not produce fine fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So then, by their fruits you will recognize them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of the heavens, but the one who does the will of my Father in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name drive out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Go away from me, you who practice lawlessness.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a sensible man who built his house on the rock.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The rain came down, the torrents came, the winds blew and fell upon that house, yet it did not fall, for its foundation had been laid on the rock.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The rain came down, the torrents came, the winds blew and struck against that house, and it fell, and great was its fall.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astounded at his teaching,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was teaching them as one who has authority, and not as their scribes.

notes.note: The word means a heavy structural timber such as a roof beam, while the 'speck' is a tiny bit of chaff, straw or wood. The contrast is deliberately absurd: someone with a rafter in his eye offers to remove a splinter from another's.

Dogs in this setting were scavengers rather than pets, and pigs were unclean animals; both were stock images of what is unfit for sacred things. 'What is holy' may call to mind consecrated food from the temple offerings, which was not to be given to animals. Many interpreters read the saying as a crossed pattern, with the pigs trampling and the dogs turning to attack. Whom the saying has in view is disputed.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 21 ('kingdom of the heavens', 'Father in the heavens'), reflecting a Semitic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have recognized. Most English translations flatten it to the singular 'heaven'. The plural is kept here because the Greek has it.

'The Law and the Prophets' was a common way of referring to the Jewish Scriptures as a whole by their two main divisions. Jesus presents this rule as a summary of what they require. A negative form of the saying, not doing to others what you would hate, was already known in Jewish tradition, for example in Tobit 4:15.

Manuscripts divide here between a word meaning 'for' or 'because' and one giving an exclamation, 'How narrow is the gate!' The SBLGNT prints the first, which is translated here. Many manuscripts and several modern editions have the exclamation. The sense of the passage is little affected.

The participle means 'pressed' or 'squeezed'. It can describe a road that is physically tight, the natural opposite of the 'spacious' road in verse 13, and that is the reading taken here. The same verb is the ordinary word for being afflicted or oppressed, so some translations render 'the way is hard', and a hearer may well have caught both senses.
'That day' is shorthand, drawn from the prophets, for the day of God's final judgment. Jesus here casts himself as the one before whom people plead on that day and who gives the verdict.

notes.traditional: ye that work iniquity / you workers of lawlessness
notes.note: The dismissal echoes Psalm 6:8 in its Greek form, 'Depart from me, all you who work lawlessness.' The Greek noun means disregard for God's law, which is sharper than the older English 'iniquity'. The charge is pointed, since those addressed claim impressive religious achievements in Jesus' name.

Most translations have 'wise'. The Greek word is not the usual term for wisdom (sophos). It describes practical good sense, the prudence of someone who thinks ahead and acts accordingly. 'Sensible' keeps that distinction and suits a builder who chooses his site with the storm in mind.

notes.phrase: when Jesus had finished these words
notes.traditional: when Jesus had ended these sayings
notes.note: This formula, more literally 'and it happened, when Jesus finished these words', closes each of the five great blocks of teaching in Matthew (here and at 11:1, 13:53, 19:1 and 26:1). It marks the end of the discourse that began at 5:1, traditionally called the Sermon on the Mount.

In the Jewish setting of the Gospels, scribes were not copyists but trained experts in the Law of Moses, who taught and interpreted it. The contrast is usually understood this way: they taught by appeal to Scripture and to received interpretation, whereas Jesus speaks on his own authority ('but I say to you').

candidates.reason: The word is frequent across the Gospels and Acts, and 'scribes' suggests copyists to modern readers, whereas 'teachers of the law' or 'legal scholars' are live alternatives that should not vary from chapter to chapter.
The word is pervasive, and the choice between 'brother', 'brother or sister' and 'fellow believer' for the non-literal sense needs one policy for the whole New Testament.
In the plural, for deeds, translators vary between 'miracles', 'mighty works', 'works of power' and 'powers', and the word recurs throughout the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
It recurs in Matthew, Luke and Paul and is usually merged with σοφός as 'wise', so a fixed distinct rendering ('sensible', 'prudent', 'shrewd') would keep the two words apart consistently.
It recurs in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and 1 John, and translations vary between 'lawlessness', 'iniquity', 'wickedness' and 'evildoing', which obscures the link to the Law.
